transcript:
NUMBERED FACT LIST FROM ORIGINAL GUIDE (artifact/GUIDE.md):

F1: Store four litres per person per day.
F2: This equals twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours.
F3: Half for drinking, half for cooking and basic hygiene.
F4: Replace stored water every six months.
F5: Keep non-perishable, no-cook food: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, shelf-stable milk.
F6: Eat in order: perishable food from the refrigerator first, then the freezer, and only then the emergency shelf.
F7: An unopened refrigerator about four hours.
F8: A full freezer about forty-eight hours.
F9: A half-full freezer about twenty-four hours.
F10: Discard any perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius.
F11: Primary source: battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps.
F12: Avoid candles entirely, since they are a leading cause of house fires during outages.
F13: Store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each light.
F14: Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window.
F15: Each produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal.
F16: Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep.
F17: If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot maintain warmth, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.
F18: Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts.
F19: A full modern power bank of twenty thousand milliamp-hours will recharge a typical phone roughly four times.
F20: (Redundant with F19; extracted as single fact about the capacity and recharge count.)
F21: At the start of the outage, put your phone in low-power mode.
F22: Keep a seven-day supply of every prescription medication.
F23: Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remains usable at room temperature for up to twenty-eight days.
F24: Write the phone numbers of your pharmacy, your doctor, and the poison-control line on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.
F25: Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, so the grid can stabilise.
F26: If food still contains ice crystals, it can be safely refrozen.
F27: Restock everything used during the outage within one week.
F28: Start with water and batteries.
F29: Assumes a temperate climate.
F30: Lasting up to seventy-two hours.
F31: No backup generator.
F32: Work the sections in order; the earlier ones matter most.

Assumes a temperate climate and no backup generator. Work the sections in order; the earlier ones matter most.\n\n## Water\n- Store four litres per person per day = twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours; half for drinking, half for cooking and basic hygiene.\n- Use food-grade containers kept out of direct sunlight; replace stored water every six months.\n- If a storm is forecast and you have advance warning, also fill the bathtub — that water is for flushing toilets and washing, never for drinking.\n\n## Food\n- Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable, no-cook food for three days: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, shelf-stable milk.\n- Own a manual can opener, because an electric one will be useless.\n- Eat in order: perishable food from the refrigerator first, then the freezer, and only then the emergency shelf.\n\n## Refrigerator and freezer\n- Safe holding times: an unopened refrigerator about four hours; a full freezer about forty-eight hours; a half-full freezer about twenty-four hours.\n- Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a reminder note to each door.\n- Keep the freezer consolidated and full, even if some space is containers of frozen water.\n- Discard any perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius; when in doubt, throw it out.\n\n## Light\n- Primary source: battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps. Avoid candles entirely, since they are a leading cause of house fires during outages.\n- Store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each light.\n- Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen; place them where they can be found in the dark.\n\n## Heat and safety\n- Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window: each produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal.\n- Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep.\n- In cold weather, choose one small room on a south-facing side of the home, close its door, and gather everyone there; layered clothing and blankets are safer than any improvised heater.\n- If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot maintain warmth, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.\n\n## Communication and information\n- Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and know your local emergency station's frequency before the outage begins.\n- When a storm is forecast, charge every phone and power bank; a full modern power bank of twenty thousand milliamp-hours will recharge a typical phone roughly four times.\n- At the start of the outage, put your phone in low-power mode.\n- Agree in advance on one out-of-area contact whom every member of the household will text, because texts get through congested networks more reliably than voice calls.\n\n## Medical needs\n- Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, and rotate them so they stay in date.\n- Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remains usable at room temperature for up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your specific medication with a pharmacist before an emergency.\n- Write the phone numbers of your pharmacy, your doctor, and the poison-control line on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.\n\n## When the power returns\n- Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, so the grid can stabilise.\n- Check the freezer: if food still contains ice crystals, it can be safely refrozen.\n- Restock everything used during the outage within one week, starting with water and batteries.\n- Write a one-page note about what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one of those gaps before the next outage arrives.\n"}
